THE SINGULAR LIMIT OF A CHEMOTAXIS-GROWTH SYSTEM WITH GENERAL INITIAL DATA

Abstract

We study the singular limit of a system of partial differential equations which is a model for an aggregation of amoebae subjected to three effects: diffusion, growth and chemotaxis. The limit problem involves motion by mean curvature together with a nonlocal drift term. We consider rather general initial data. We prove a generation of interface property and study the motion of interface. We also obtain an optimal estimate of the thickness and the location of the transition layer that develops.11 1 AMS Subject Classifications: 35K57, 35B50, 35R35, 92C17.

MATTHIEU ALFARO

Analyse Numérique et EDP, Université de Paris Sud,

91405 Orsay Cedex, France.

1 Introduction

Let us start by a short description of life-cycles of the cellular slime molds (amoebae). The cells feed and divide until exhaustion of food supply. Then, the amoebae aggregate to form a multicellular assembly called a slug. It migrates to a new location, then forms into a fruiting body, consisting of a stalk formed from dead amoebae and spores on the top (fruiting bodies that are visible to the naked eye are often referred to as mushrooms). Under suitable conditions of moisture, temperature, spores release new amoebae. The cycle then repeats itself.

It is known that the aggregation stage is mediated by chemotaxis, i.e. the tendency of biological individuals to direct their movements according to certain chemicals in their environment. The chemotactant (acrasin) is produced by the amoebae themselves and degraded by an extracellular enzyme (acrasinase). For more details on the biological background, we refer to [15], [20] or [10].

So the amoebae have a random motion analogous to diffusion coupled with an oriented chemotactic motion in the direction of a positive gradient of acrasin. In 1970, Keller and Segel [15] proposed the following system as a model to describe such movements leading to slime mold aggregation:

(K​S){ut=∇⋅(D2∇u)−∇⋅(D1∇v),vt=Dv​Δ​v+f⁡(v)​u−k⁡(v)​v,(KS)\quad\begin{cases}u_{t}&=\nabla\cdot(D_{2}\nabla u)-\nabla\cdot(D_{1}\nabla v),\\ v_{t}&=D_{v}\Delta v+f(v)u-k(v)v,\end{cases}

inside a closed region Ω\Omega. Here, uu, respectively vv, denotes the concentration of amoebae, respectively of acrasin; f⁡(v)f(v) is the production rate of acrasin, and k⁡(v)k(v) the degradation rate of acrasin (due to acrasinase); D2=D2​(u,v)D_{2}=D_{2}(u,v), respectively D1=D1​(u,v)D_{1}=D_{1}(u,v), measures the vigor of the random motion of the amoebae, respectively the strength of the influence of the acrasin gradient on the flow of amoebae; DvD_{v} is a positive and constant diffusion coefficient. The problem is completed by initial data u0u_{0} and v0v_{0} and, assuming that there is now flow of the amoebae or the acrasin across the boundary ∂Ω\partial\Omega, by homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions

∇u⋅ν=∇v⋅ν=0on∂Ω×(0,+∞),\nabla u\cdot\nu=\nabla v\cdot\nu=0\quad\ \textrm{on}\ \;\partial\Omega\times(0,+\infty),

ν\nu being the unit outward normal to ∂Ω\partial\Omega.

An often used simplified model is obtained as follows. By some receptor mechanism, cells do not measure the gradient of vv but of some χ⁡(v)\chi(v), with a sensitive function χ\chi satisfying χ′>0\chi^{\prime}>0, so that D1​(u,v)=u​χ′​(v)D_{1}(u,v)=u\chi^{\prime}(v). By taking D2D_{2}, ff and kk as constant functions and using some rescaling arguments, the system reduces to

(K​S′){ut=duΔu−∇⋅(u∇χ(v)),τ​vt=dv​Δ​v+u−γ​v,(KS\,^{\prime})\quad\begin{cases}\;\;u_{t}&=d_{u}\Delta u-\nabla\cdot(u\nabla\chi(v)),\\ \tau v_{t}&=d_{v}\Delta v+u-\gamma v,\end{cases}

with dud_{u}, dvd_{v}, τ\tau and γ\gamma some positive constants.

Many analyses of the Keller-Segel model for the aggregation process were proposed. Chemotaxis having some features of “negative diffusion”, Nanjundiah [20] suggests that the whole population concentrates in a single point; we refer to this phenomenon as the chemotactic collapse. In mathematical terms, this amounts to blow up in finite time. As a matter of fact, it turns out that the possibility of collapse depends upon the space dimension. In particular it never happens in the one-dimensional case whereas in two space dimensions, assuming radially symmetric situations, it only occurs if the total amoebae number is sufficiently large. The problem of global existence and blow up of solutions has been intensively studied; we refer in particular to [9], [22], [16], [13], [19], [11], [12].

In a different framework, Mimura and Tsujikawa [17], consider aggregating pattern-dynamics arising in the following chemotaxis model with growth:

(M​Tε){ut=ε2Δu−ε∇⋅(u∇χ(v))+f(u),τ​vt=Δ​v+u−γ​v,(MT^{\varepsilon})\quad\begin{cases}\;\;u_{t}&=\varepsilon^{2}\Delta u-\varepsilon\nabla\cdot(u\nabla\chi(v))+f(u),\\ \tau v_{t}&=\Delta v+u-\gamma v,\end{cases}

where ε>0\varepsilon>0 is a small parameter. The function ff is cubic, 0 and 1 being its stable zeros, and satisfies ∫01f>0\int_{0}^{1}f>0. In this model, the population is subjected to three effects: diffusion, growth and chemotaxis. The diffusion rate and the chemotactic rate are both very small compared with the growth rate. They observe that, in a first stage, internal layers — which describe the boundaries of aggregating regions — develop; in a second stage, the motion of the aggregating regions — which can be described by that of internal layers — takes place. The balance of the three effects (diffusion, growth and chemotaxis) makes the aggregation mechanism possible. Taking the limit ε→0\varepsilon\to 0, they formally derive the equation for the motion of the limit interface and study the stability of radially symmetric equilibrium solutions.

The purpose of this paper is to extend some of the results obtained by Bonami, Hilhorst, Logak and Mimura [4] about the singular limit of a variant of system (M​Tε)(MT^{\varepsilon}), where the second equation is elliptic (τ=0\tau=0):

(Pε){ut=Δu−∇⋅(u∇χ(v))+1ε2fε(u) in ​Ω×(0,+∞),0=Δ​v+u−γ​v in ​Ω×(0,+∞),∂u∂ν=∂v∂ν=0 on ​∂Ω×(0,+∞),u​(x,0)=u0​(x) in ​Ω,(P^{\varepsilon})\quad\begin{cases}u_{t}=\Delta u-\nabla\cdot(u\nabla\chi(v))+\displaystyle{\frac{1}{\varepsilon^{2}}}f_{\varepsilon}(u)&\textrm{ in }\Omega\times(0,+\infty),\\ 0=\Delta v+u-\gamma v&\textrm{ in }\Omega\times(0,+\infty),\\ \displaystyle{\frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}}=\displaystyle{\frac{\partial v}{\partial\nu}}=0&\textrm{ on }\partial\Omega\times(0,+\infty),\\ u(x,0)=u_{0}(x)&\textrm{ in }\Omega,\end{cases}

where Ω\Omega is a smooth bounded domain in ℝN\mathbb{R}^{N} (N≥2N\geq 2), ν\nu is the Euclidian unit normal vector exterior to ∂Ω\partial\Omega. We assume that γ\gamma is a positive constant and that the nonlinearityfεf_{\varepsilon} is given by

Bonami, Hilhorst, Logak and Mimura [4] have proved a motion of interface property; more precisely, for some prepared initial data, they show that (uε,vε)(u^{\varepsilon},v^{\varepsilon}) converges to (u0,v0)(u^{0},v^{0}) as ε→0\varepsilon\rightarrow 0, on the interval (0,T)(0,T). So the evolution of Γt\Gamma_{t} determines the aggregating patterns of the individuals. Here we consider the case of arbitrary initial data. Our first main result, Theorem 1.3, describes the profile of the solution after a very short initial period. It asserts that, given a virtually arbitrary initial datum u0u_{0}, the solution uεu^{\varepsilon} quickly becomes close to 11 or 00, except in a small neighborhood of the initial interface Γ0\Gamma_{0}, creating a steep transition layer around Γ0\Gamma_{0} (generation of interface). The time needed to develop such a transition layer, which we will denote by tεt^{\varepsilon}, is of order ε2​|ln⁡ε|\varepsilon^{2}|\ln\varepsilon|. The theorem then states that the solution uεu^{\varepsilon} remains close to the step function u0u^{0} on the time interval [tε,T][t^{\varepsilon},T] (motion of interface). Moreover, as is clear from the estimates in the theorem, the “thickness” of the transition layer is of order ε\varepsilon.

As ε→0\varepsilon\to 0, the solution (uε,vε)(u^{\varepsilon},v^{\varepsilon}) converges to (u0,v0)(u^{0},v^{0}) everywhere in ⋃0<t≤T(Ωt(0​or​ 1)×{t})\bigcup_{0<t\leq T}(\Omega^{(0\ \text{or}\ 1)}_{t}\times\{t\}).

As far as we know, the best thickness estimate in the literature was of order ε​|ln⁡ε|\varepsilon|\ln\varepsilon| (see [5], [6]). The organization of this paper is as follows. Section 2 is devoted to preliminaries: we recall the method of asymptotic expansions to derive the equation of the interface motion; we also recall a relaxed comparison principle used in [4]. In Section 3, we prove a generation of interface property. The corresponding sub- and super-solutions are constructed by modifying the solution of the ordinary differential equation ut=ε−2​f​(u)u_{t}=\varepsilon^{-2}f(u), obtained by neglecting diffusion and chemotaxis. In Section 4, in order to study the motion of interface, we construct a pair of sub- and super-solutions that rely on a related one-dimensional stationary problem. Finally, in Section 5, by fitting the two pairs of sub- and super-solutions into each other, we prove Theorem 1.3, Theorem 1.5 and theirs corollaries.

2 Some preliminaries

2.1 Formal derivation

A formal derivation of the equation of interface motion was given in [3]. Nevertheless we briefly present it in a slightly different way: we use arguments similar to those in [21] where the first two terms of the asymptotic expansion determine the interface equation. The observations we make here will help the rigorous analysis in later sections, in particular for the construction of sub- and super-solutions for the study of the motion of interface in Section 4.

Let (uε,vε)(u^{\varepsilon},v^{\varepsilon}) be the solution of Problem (Pε)(P^{\;\!\varepsilon}). 2.2 A comparison principle

The definition of sub- and super-solutions is the one proposed in [4].

Definition 2.2.

Let (uε−,uε+)(u_{\varepsilon}^{-},u_{\varepsilon}^{+}) be two smooth functions with uε−≤uε+u_{\varepsilon}^{-}\leq u_{\varepsilon}^{+} on QTQ_{T} and

∂uε−∂ν≤0≤∂uε+∂νon​∂Ω×(0,T).\frac{\partial u_{\varepsilon}^{-}}{\partial\nu}\leq 0\leq\frac{\partial u_{\varepsilon}^{+}}{\partial\nu}\quad\ \text{on}\;\ \partial\Omega\times(0,T).

By definition, (uε−,uε+)(u_{\varepsilon}^{-},u_{\varepsilon}^{+}) is a pair of sub- and super-solutions if, for any vεv^{\varepsilon} which satisfies

{uε−≤−Δ​vε+γ​vε≤uε+ on ​QT,∂vε∂ν=0 on ​∂Ω×(0,T),\begin{cases}u_{\varepsilon}^{-}\leq-\Delta v^{\varepsilon}+\gamma v^{\varepsilon}\leq u_{\varepsilon}^{+}\quad&\text{ on }Q_{T},\\ \displaystyle{\frac{\partial v^{\varepsilon}}{\partial\nu}}=0\quad&\text{ on }\partial\Omega\times(0,T),\end{cases} (2.11)

we have

Lvε​[uε−]≤0≤Lvε​[uε+],L_{v^{\varepsilon}}[u_{\varepsilon}^{-}]\leq 0\leq L_{v^{\varepsilon}}[u_{\varepsilon}^{+}],

where the operator LvεL_{v^{\varepsilon}} is defined by

Lvε[ϕ]=ϕt−Δϕ+∇⋅(ϕ∇χ(vε))−1ε2fε(ϕ).L_{v^{\varepsilon}}[\phi]=\phi_{t}-\Delta\phi+\nabla\cdot(\phi\nabla\chi(v^{\varepsilon}))-\displaystyle{\frac{1}{\varepsilon^{2}}}f_{\varepsilon}(\phi).

As proved in [4], the following comparison principle holds.

Proposition 2.3.

Let a pair of sub- and super-solutions be given. Assume that, for all x∈Ωx\in\Omega,

uε−​(x,0)≤u0​(x)≤uε+​(x,0).u_{\varepsilon}^{-}(x,0)\leq u_{0}(x)\leq u_{\varepsilon}^{+}(x,0).

Then, if we denote by (uε,vε)(u^{\varepsilon},v^{\varepsilon}) the solution of Problem (Pε)(P^{\;\!\varepsilon}), the function uεu^{\varepsilon} satisfies, for all (x,t)∈QT(x,t)\in Q_{T},

uε−​(x,t)≤uε​(x,t)≤uε+​(x,t).u_{\varepsilon}^{-}(x,t)\leq u^{\varepsilon}(x,t)\leq u_{\varepsilon}^{+}(x,t).

3 Generation of interface

In this section we study the rapid formation of internal layers in a neighborhood of Γ0={x∈Ω,u0​(x)=1/2}\Gamma_{0}=\{x\in\Omega,u_{0}(x)=1/2\} within a very short time interval of order ε2​|ln⁡ε|\varepsilon^{2}|\ln\varepsilon|. In the sequel, we shall always assume that 0<η<1/40<\eta<1/4. The main result of this section is the following.

Theorem 3.1.

Let η\eta be arbitrary and define μ\mu as the derivative of f⁡(u)f(u) at the unstable equilibrium u=1/2u=1/2, that is

μ=f′​(1/2)=1/4.\mu=f^{\prime}(1/2)=1/4. (3.1)

Then there exist positive constants ε0\varepsilon_{0} and M0M_{0} such that, for all ε∈(0,ε0)\,\varepsilon\in(0,\varepsilon_{0}),

  • •

    for all x∈Ωx\in\Omega,

    −η≤uε​(x,μ−1​ε2​|ln⁡ε|)≤1+η,-\eta\leq u^{\varepsilon}(x,\mu^{-1}\varepsilon^{2}|\ln\varepsilon|)\leq 1+\eta, (3.2)
  • •

    for all x∈Ωx\in\Omega such that |u0​(x)−12|≥M0​ε|u_{0}(x)-\frac{1}{2}|\geq M_{0}\varepsilon, we have that

    if​u0​(x)≥1/2+M0​ε​then​uε​(x,μ−1​ε2​|ln⁡ε|)≥1−η,\displaystyle\text{if}\;~~u_{0}(x)\geq 1/2+M_{0}\varepsilon\;~~\text{then}\;~~u^{\varepsilon}(x,\mu^{-1}\varepsilon^{2}|\ln\varepsilon|)\geq 1-\eta, (3.3)
    if​u0​(x)≤1/2−M0​ε​then​uε​(x,μ−1​ε2​|ln⁡ε|)≤η.\displaystyle\text{if}\;~~u_{0}(x)\leq 1/2-M_{0}\varepsilon\;~~\text{then}\;~~u^{\varepsilon}(x,\mu^{-1}\varepsilon^{2}|\ln\varepsilon|)\leq\eta. (3.4)

The above theorem will be proved by constructing a suitable pair of sub and super-solutions.

4 Motion of interface

We have seen in Section 3 that, after a very short time, the solution uεu^{\varepsilon} develops a clear transition layer. In the present section, we show that it persists and that its law of motion is well approximated by the interface equation in (P0)(P^{0}) obtained by formal asymptotic expansions in subsection 2.1.

More precisely, take the first term of the formal asymptotic expansion (2.3) as a formal expansion of the solution:

uε​(x,t)≈u~ε​(x,t):=U0​(d~​(x,t)ε),u^{\varepsilon}(x,t)\,\approx\,\tilde{u}^{\varepsilon}(x,t):=U_{0}\Big(\frac{\widetilde{d}(x,t)}{\varepsilon}\Big), (4.1)

where U0U_{0} is defined in (2.6). The right-hand side is a function having a well-developed transition layer, and its interface lies exactly on Γt\Gamma_{t}. We show that this function is a good approximation of the solution; more precisely:

If uεu^{\varepsilon} becomes very close to u~ε\tilde{u}^{\varepsilon} at some time moment t=t0t=t_{0}, then it stays close to u~ε\tilde{u}^{\varepsilon} for the rest of time. Consequently, Γtε\Gamma^{\varepsilon}_{t} evolves roughly like Γt\Gamma_{t}.

To that purpose, we will construct a pair of sub- and super-solutions uε−u_{\varepsilon}^{-} and uε+u_{\varepsilon}^{+} for Problem (Pε)(P^{\varepsilon}) by slightly modifying u~ε\tilde{u}^{\varepsilon}. It then follows that, if the solution uεu^{\varepsilon} satisfies

uε−​(x,t0)≤uε​(x,t0)≤uε+​(x,t0),u_{\varepsilon}^{-}(x,t_{0})\leq u^{\varepsilon}(x,t_{0})\leq u_{\varepsilon}^{+}(x,t_{0}),

for some t0≥0t_{0}\geq 0, then

uε−​(x,t)≤uε​(x,t)≤uε+​(x,t),u_{\varepsilon}^{-}(x,t)\leq u^{\varepsilon}(x,t)\leq u_{\varepsilon}^{+}(x,t),

5 Proof of the main results

In this section, we prove our main results by fitting the two pairs of sub- and super-solutions, constructed for the study of the generation and the motion of interface, into each other.

Since C′>CC^{\prime}>C and since the curvature of Γt\Gamma_{t} is uniformly bounded as tt varies over [0,T][0,T], we see that, if ε0\varepsilon_{0} is sufficiently small,

x(0)∈Ωt(0)∖𝒩C​ε​(Γt)andx(1)∈Ωt(1)∖𝒩C​ε​(Γt).x^{(0)}\in\Omega^{(0)}_{t}\setminus\mathcal{N}_{C\varepsilon}(\Gamma_{t})\quad\text{and}\quad x^{(1)}\in\Omega^{(1)}_{t}\setminus\mathcal{N}_{C\varepsilon}(\Gamma_{t}).

Therefore, if t∈[μ−1​ε2​|ln⁡ε|,T]t\in[\mu^{-1}\varepsilon^{2}|\ln\varepsilon|,T], then, by Theorem 1.3, we have

uε​(x(0),t)<1/2<uε​(x(1),t).u^{\varepsilon}(x^{(0)},t)<1/2<u^{\varepsilon}(x^{(1)},t). (5.17)

On the other hand, if t∈[0,μ−1​ε2​|ln⁡ε|]t\in[0,\mu^{-1}\varepsilon^{2}|\ln\varepsilon|], then from (5.13), (5.15) and the fact that C′>C~C^{\prime}>\tilde{C}, we again obtain (5.17). Thus (5.17) holds for all t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T]. Now, by the mean value theorem, we see that, for each t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T], there exists a point x~\tilde{x} such that

x~∈[x(0),x(1)]anduε​(x~,t)=1/2.\tilde{x}\in[x^{(0)},x^{(1)}]\quad\text{and}\quad u^{\varepsilon}(\tilde{x},t)=1/2.

This implies x~∈Γtε\tilde{x}\in\Gamma_{t}^{\varepsilon}. Furthermore we have |x0−x~|≤C′​ε|x_{0}-\tilde{x}|\leq C^{\prime}\varepsilon, since x~\tilde{x} lies on the line segment [x(0),x(1)][x^{(0)},x^{(1)}]. This proves (5.16). ∎
